clue.text: 'Labour united with Brenda' cover-up

parts.note: to labour is to toil, to sweat
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose royal cipher is ER

explanation.surface: A political scandal: some deal between the Labour Party and the Queen being hushed up.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called Queen Elizabeth 'Brenda'; ER (Elizabeth Regina) is the usual crossword Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweater is a knitted garment pulled over the torso, so it literally covers you up.

clue.text: see 4dn.
Alliance let Kinnock's no. 1 off

indicators.note: a letter let off is let go, dropped from the word in front of it

parts.note: let in its old sense is a hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance', so to let is to obstruct or block

indicators.note: number one of a name is its opening letter

parts.note: Neil Kinnock, former Labour leader, supplies his initial

explanation.surface: A coalition that let the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock off the hook.
explanation.walkthrough: BLOCK loses its K to leave BLOC; 'let' meaning obstruct is an archaic sense kept alive in legal phrases and tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of nations or parties combined for a common political purpose, an alliance.

clue.text: (& 2dn.) Abandoned as useless, Corbyn and his ilk — he felt no different about similar half-soaked leaders

parts.note: Jeremy Corbyn and his supporters are the political left

indicators.note: made different means the letters are rearranged into another order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: leaders are the front letters of the words just before

parts.note: the first letter of similar
the first letter of half-soaked

explanation.surface: A jibe that Corbyn's wing of Labour has been discarded, with some sneer about soggy leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram takes HE FELT NO plus S and H from 'similar half-soaked' to give ON THE SHELF after LEFT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something left on the shelf has been put aside and is no longer wanted, idiomatically discarded as of no use.

clue.text: Ignorant reactionary's embarrassed snog

parts.note: embarrassment makes you go red
to snog is British slang for kissing passionately, to neck

explanation.surface: A bigot blushing over a passionate kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: Redneck is a derogatory label, originally American, for a narrow-minded, uneducated, politically backward person.

clue.text: Sting wrong to throttle wife — led off

indicators.note: throttling grips something round the neck, so one word wraps around another

parts.note: a wrong is a sin
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

indicators.note: something gone off has gone bad or awry, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A crime report: a man strangles his wife and is led away by police.
explanation.walkthrough: SIN holds W to give SWIN, then the jumbled LED supplies DLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sting is slang for a confidence trick or fraud, a swindle.

clue.text: Rest uneasy about member's horsey affair

indicators.note: about means placed around, so one piece goes round the other
uneasy suggests restless and unsettled, so these letters will not stay in order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a limb is a member of the body

explanation.surface: A restless night over some politician's equestrian scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' is a limb here, not an MP. The St Leger is a classic flat horse race run each September at Doncaster in England.
explanation.definitionFit: The St Leger is a famous horse race, so it is literally an event, or affair, involving horses.

clue.text: Wartime pals of male, having whole caboodle packed into trusses

indicators.note: packed into means placed inside something else

parts.note: to truss is to tie up, so trusses are ties
he is the male pronoun
the whole caboodle means everything, all

explanation.surface: A man's old war buddies all strapped into something, perhaps a hernia truss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trusses' suggests a surgical support, but it is a verb noun for things that bind.
explanation.definitionFit: The Allies were the nations, Britain, America and the Soviet Union among them, fighting together against the Axis in the Second World War.

clue.text: Heading for oblivion, like post-referendum Britain

definitions.meaning: first meaning: declining, soon to be obsolete
second meaning: literally in the process of leaving, as Britain was leaving the EU after the 2016 Brexit vote

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is figurative decline; the second is literal departure, and the satire is that both fit Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both fading into obsolescence and physically departing, matching the decline and the Brexit exit.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Drug character much evident in Twitter messages

definitions.text: character much evident in Twitter messages

parts.note: hash is short for hashish, cannabis resin
a character is a written symbol, a sign

explanation.surface: A dodgy character who tweets a lot about drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' does double duty: it is the second piece of wordplay and the head of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The hash sign, #, marks hashtags, which appear constantly in tweets to tag topics.

clue.text: Maybe Boris gets his party to assess "a new temperature"

parts.note: Boris Johnson's party is the Conservatives, abbreviated CON
to test is to assess
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
T is the symbol for temperature

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's party is asked to judge some fresh political heat.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2016 Boris Johnson was a contender in the Conservative leadership race; 'Maybe' signals the definition is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Johnson, as a leadership hopeful, is one example of a contestant, someone competing in a contest.

clue.text: Down to your undies for punishment?

wordplay.note: someone stripped to their underwear is wearing fewer clothes; read the letters as a two-word phrase

explanation.surface: A schoolroom threat of being made to strip for a punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as LESS ON: someone down to their underwear has less on.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesson can be a salutary experience or rebuke, as in 'that will teach you a lesson', so a punishment.

clue.text: Dotty (Lab.) gave in, so may be passed over

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for an adjective: navigable describes what may be passed over

indicators.note: dotty means crazy, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A batty Labour woman conceded, so she may be overlooked for promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passed over' looks like being ignored for a job, but here it is sailing over water.
explanation.definitionFit: A navigable river or sea is one ships can travel across, so it may be passed over by boat.

clue.text: Nick Henry, pressed against female — creep!

indicators.note: pressed against means placed right next to, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: Hal is a pet name for Henry, as in Shakespeare's Prince Hal
F is the abbreviation for female
to creep is to inch along

explanation.surface: Henry is arrested after pressing himself against a woman, and called a creep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick Henry' reads as 'arrest Henry'; Nick is the definition. Half-inch is Cockney rhyming slang: half-inch rhymes with pinch, meaning steal.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang half-inch stands for pinch, and to pinch or nick is to steal.

clue.text: Scottish finally in a mutiny — terrible barbarism!

indicators.note: terrible suggests a dreadful mess, so these letters are thrown into disorder
finally points to the very last letter of the word

parts.note: the final letter of Scottish
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation at the savagery of a mutiny among Scottish troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhumanity is extreme cruelty, a lack of compassion, which is what barbarism describes.

clue.text: VIP, loaded, with crew

parts.note: something loaded is heavy
W is the abbreviation for with
a rowing eight is a crew

explanation.surface: A rich celebrity arrives with an entourage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loaded' tempts as rich, but here it means weighed down.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavyweight is an important, influential person, figuratively one of great weight.

clue.text: Right out of large fancy underwear? That's very symbolic

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase rather than a noun: it describes the subject

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or ornamental, so the letters are reworked
out of means taken away from what follows

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
a bra is an item of underwear

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on the deep meaning of a big frilly bra.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R from LARGE, jumble the remaining LAGE into ALGE, then add BRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Algebra is the branch of mathematics that uses letters and symbols for numbers, so it is thoroughly symbolic.

clue.text: Strong line taken with enclosure that's stuffy

parts.note: f is forte, the musical direction for loud or strong
a row is a line
a sty is an enclosure for pigs

explanation.surface: A firm policy on fencing livestock that seems old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Frowsty is a British word for a room that is warm, stale and airless, which is stuffy.

clue.text: Conservative has-been, worn out by gloom and extremes of envy

parts.note: worn out things are old
fog is a murky gloom

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two outermost letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of envy

explanation.surface: A washed-up Tory, exhausted by depression and jealousy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservative' looks like a capital-C Tory, but the definition means anyone old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: An old fogey is a person stuck in old-fashioned ways and resistant to change, a dated conservative type.

clue.text: Depressed Britain in clutches of indeterminate number

indicators.note: held in the clutches of means gripped inside something else

parts.note: some denotes an unspecified quantity
BR is an abbreviation for Britain

explanation.surface: A gloomy Britain held in the grip of an unknown number of forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Sombre describes a dark, gloomy, melancholy mood, close to depressed or dejected.

clue.text: In with Gore-Bush soft soap

indicators.note: soft means pliable, so the letters can be squashed into a new shape

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Being cosy with Al Gore and George Bush through flattering talk, soft soap being smooth flattery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soft soap' reads as one phrase for flattery; split it into the indicator and the definition. Neighbours is a long-running Australian TV soap opera hugely popular in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Neighbours is the Australian television soap opera set in Ramsay Street, so it is an example of a soap.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) Goes down swimmingly, you'll be glad to hear

indicators.note: swimming letters float about and settle in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Something is going down well, which is pleasing to report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes down swimmingly' reads as an idiom for going well; split it into fodder and anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Good news is information people are pleased to receive, by definition welcome tidings.

clue.text: see 10ac.
see 22dn.
Shady newspaper chief is after staff

indicators.note: is after means comes behind, so this piece is placed second

parts.note: a crook is a shepherd's staff
the chief of a newspaper is the editor, ED

explanation.surface: A dodgy newspaper editor is pursuing his employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' suggests employees, but it is a shepherd's stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Crooked means dishonest or underhand, as shady dealings are of doubtful honesty.

clue.text: Following Archer's lead, bastard gets tucked in stir

indicators.note: following means coming behind, so the next piece goes after the first
a lead is the front, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the initial of Archer
git is British slang for a contemptible person
to tuck in is to eat heartily

explanation.surface: Jeffrey Archer's example is followed by a villain who ends up in prison, stir being slang for jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stir' suggests prison, which fits Jeffrey Archer, the novelist jailed for perjury; but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir is to mix by moving around, which is what agitating a liquid does; agitate also means to rouse.
